Fictional source summary:
Researchers recruited 45 volunteers from one urban cycling club. Thirty-one said they preferred protected cycle lanes. The study did not sample non-cyclists, other clubs, or residents in other locations.

Draft passage:
The interviews show that most residents prefer protected cycle lanes. Since 31 of the 45 participants supported them, the findings establish broad public demand across the city.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The paragraph reports a preference count from the participant sample. A volunteer sample from one cycling club cannot establish the preferences of all city residents. The numerator describes the sample, not the population. Limit the conclusion to the sampled club members and identify the missing population coverage.
<answer>revise</answer>

Fictional source summary:
A proposed analysis selects 16 discussion threads and codes five replies within each thread. Replies share the opening post and may come from the same participants. The plan contains no adjustment for clustering.

Draft passage:
The analysis will use 80 independent observations because each of the 16 threads contributes five replies. Treating every reply as independent will allow a precise comparison of discussion patterns.

The sampling plan specifies thread counts and replies per thread. Eighty coded replies are not necessarily 80 independent observations. Shared thread context can create dependence. Distinguish reply count from independent units and specify how the analysis will account for thread-level clustering.
<answer>revise</answer>

Fictional source summary:
In a fictional scholarship trial, 20% of the comparison group and 30% of the reminder group submitted an application. These are application rates, not acceptance rates. No longer-term outcomes were reported.

Draft passage:
The reminder increased the application rate by 10 percent, from 20% to 30%. This comparison concerns applications rather than scholarship acceptance, and it provides no evidence about later outcomes.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The paragraph states both application rates in the comparison. The absolute difference between 20% and 30% is 10 percentage points. The relative increase is 50%, so calling it a 10 percent increase changes the quantity. Use 10 percentage points for the absolute increase, or explicitly identify 50% as the relative increase.
<answer>revise</answer>

Fictional source summary:
A university survey asked 180 volunteers how often they visited the library and how satisfied they were with their studies. Frequent visitors reported greater satisfaction. Library attendance was not assigned, and prior motivation was not measured.

Draft passage:
The survey shows that visiting the library increases student satisfaction. Frequent visitors were more satisfied, so universities can improve satisfaction by encouraging students to attend more often.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The paragraph compares library attendance with reported student satisfaction. The survey establishes an association, not a causal effect. Motivation could influence both attendance and satisfaction. Replace the causal conclusion with an association and qualify the proposed intervention as something that would need testing.
<answer>revise</answer>

Fictional source summary:
A proposed project asks whether responses address a speaker’s objections. Its current codebook records only response length and the presence of polite phrases. It does not code whether a response discusses the objection or supplies relevant reasons.

Draft passage:
The project will measure objection responsiveness through response length and polite wording. Longer and more polite replies will receive higher responsiveness scores because these features show that the concern has been answered.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The project concerns how responses engage with objections. Length and politeness do not directly measure whether a reply answers an objection. A response can be polite and long while avoiding the concern. Add criteria for engagement with the specific objection and relevant reasons; keep length and politeness as separate variables.
<answer>revise</answer>

An experiment randomly assigned 240 people to read one of two appointment reminders. Participants rated clarity immediately afterward. The revised message received higher clarity ratings. Attendance and later behavior were not measured.

Draft passage:
The revised reminder improved appointment attendance. Participants rated it as clearer than the original, showing that understandable messages make people more likely to attend.

The paragraph concerns the clarity of a revised appointment reminder. Clarity ratings are not attendance outcomes. Random assignment supports a comparison on the measured rating, not an unmeasured behavior. Describe the effect on clarity ratings and state that attendance remains untested.

A classroom pilot tested a feedback worksheet with 22 students during one assignment. Students reported that the worksheet was useful. Writing quality was not independently scored, and no comparison class was included.

Draft passage:
The worksheet should replace existing feedback methods across the university. Positive usefulness ratings from the pilot establish that it improves writing quality more than the alternatives.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The pilot provides preliminary information relevant to designing a further study. Usefulness ratings from one uncontrolled pilot do not establish improved writing quality or superiority over alternatives. Recommend further testing and name the missing outcome and comparison instead of recommending university-wide replacement.
<answer>revise</answer>

A small randomized study compared two tutoring formats. The estimated mean difference was 2 points, with a 95% confidence interval from -3 to 7. The researchers reported that the result was not statistically significant.

Draft passage:
The study proves that the two tutoring formats are equally effective. Its non-significant result means that neither format can have an advantage over the other.

Give brief feedback on evidence accuracy and a concrete next step. Do not invent faults or praise. Assess only what this source supports, not grammar or personal style. Finish with <answer>revise</answer> if an evidence correction is needed, otherwise <answer>retain</answer>.

The paragraph focuses on the comparison between the tutoring formats. A non-significant result does not prove equivalence. The interval includes both zero and differences that could matter. Report the uncertainty and the absence of a detected difference rather than claiming that the formats are equal.
<answer>revise</answer>
